papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.27--0.50m in bipedal locomotion and 0.50--0.20m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/REACH/.
authors: Shengzhang Xu, Yuning Guo, Weiyi Hu, Yifeng Xu, Zhongyu Li, He Kong
bullets: Addresses the limitation of bipedal systems that cannot traverse spaces below crouched-walking clearance.
Uses hierarchical reinforcement learning with history-conditioned latent representations for contact-rich crawling.
Employs a bidirectional transition policy to connect crouched walking and crawling despite major kinematic and contact changes.
Combines learned locomotion skills with LiDAR-based 3D planning and proactive body-height commands.
Real-world experiments show accurate tracking, terrain robustness, reliable mode transitions, and confined-space traversal.

papers.abstract: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.
authors: Riccardo Bianco, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses precise timing, alignment, and collision avoidance when flying through moving narrow gaps.

Pathwise gradients outperform score-function gradients in controlled precision-critical benchmarks.
Achieves 99.3% simulation success and 80% success across 10 real-world trials from varied initial conditions.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure - moving contrast edges - to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64x64 event observation in 17 microseconds on a single GPU - over 400x faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline - enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes - three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty, traversability probability approx. 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. authors: Dequan Ou, Austin Lopez, Quentin Missinne, Christophe De Wagter, Guido C. H. E. de Croon

papers.abstract: In smart factory environments, passive entities such as humans and movable obstacles may interfere with autonomous robot operations, posing significant safety risks. Detecting potential conflicts between robots and entities outside their field-of-view (FoV) is therefore of paramount importance. However, conventional passive object detection systems rely on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, or cameras, which operate under direct line-of-sight (LoS) and are limited by obstacles and occlusions. To overcome these limitations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception via the communication infrastructure thanks to cooperation among distributed wireless devices. In this paper, we propose a framework for passive entity sensing beyond the robot's FoV that relies solely on distributed channel measurements from the communication infrastructure to perform risk-aware classification. These measurements are embedded into high-dimensional representations using hyperdimensional computing (HDC), enabling robust and scalable learning without explicit channel reconstruction. Numerical simulations based on a commercial ray tracer and ROS-based validation in realistic smart factory scenarios demonstrate improved safety and enhanced path planning with up to 89% accuracy under severe occlusions, while maintaining low computational complexity.
authors: Placido Mursia, Marco Rossanese, Francesco Devoti, Adrian Lendinez Ibanez, Lanfranco Zanzi, Xi Li, Xavier Costa-Perez
bullets: Addresses robot safety risks from humans and obstacles hidden by occlusions in smart factories.

Validated through ray-tracing simulations and ROS-based smart-factory scenarios.
Supports safer path planning under severe occlusions, with scope demonstrated in simulated and realistic validation environments.

papers.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
authors: Daan van Hamersveld, Ewoud Smeur, Iurii Kriachko
bullets: Addresses the need for lower-cost, longer-range interception of medium-altitude, long-endurance drones.

Outperforms two classical guidance controllers under most simulated conditions.
Successfully intercepts maneuvering fixed-wing targets in real-flight tests.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies form structured internal representations of traffic, ego behavior, and road constraints. These representations offer a monitoring interface for anticipating failures, complementing risk signals from trajectories, controls, and manually designed features. We introduce the Structured Representation Probe (SRP), a lightweight monitor that reads actor, ego, and map representations from a frozen policy. SRP learns a separate linear risk direction for each source and aggregates element scores through cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling, retaining sensitivity to salient evidence while reducing dependence on token count. Event-window supervision links the readout to upcoming hard failures, and auxiliary event type heads jointly train the source directions across failure modes. Online alerting uses a single generic score without modifying the driving policy. Bench2Drive experiments on DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD show higher frame-level PR-AUC and ROC-AUC than the evaluated runtime baselines. On DriveTransformer at a horizon of 2 seconds, ROC-AUC reaches 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency, with 2.67% readout runtime overhead. The trained probes also retain the ability to distinguish impending failures on new routes.
authors: Jiawei Liang, Tianrui Lou, Le Yang, Xianghao Jiao, Wei Wang, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Addresses the need for risk monitoring that complements trajectory-, control-, and hand-crafted-feature-based signals.
Reads actor, ego, and map representations, learning source-specific linear risk directions and combining element scores with cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling.
Uses event-window supervision and auxiliary event-type heads to train a single generic online alert score without changing the driving policy.
On Bench2Drive with DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD, SRP outperforms evaluated runtime baselines; for DriveTransformer at a 2-second horizon, ROC-AUC is 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency.
Adds 2.67% readout runtime overhead and retains failure-discrimination ability on new routes.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles in enclosed spaces such as tunnels and mines rely on range maps that smoke, dust and fog make inaccurate. Conformal prediction calibrates a keepout around the mapped walls that covers the true unsafe set at a chosen probability. Typically an unmodified planner treats the keepout as an inflated obstacle, and nothing ensures that the vehicle can stop before the keepout as it moves when sensing degrades. In narrow passages this margin and the planner's buffer close the route, and existing remedies recover reach by relaxing the coverage level. This paper conditions the conformal margin on a label-free severity estimate to hold coverage near its target as degradation varies. A planning and control layer enforces one braking-distance condition on the keepout at plan time and at every command, takes the measured tracking residual as its only margin and never alters the keepout. The keepout is validated on ground-robot smoke recordings and the closed loop in simulated quadrotor flights in a foggy tunnel against the standard deployment. In closed-loop simulation the proposed system substantially reduces entries into the calibrated keepout and reaches numerically more goals than the deployment pattern in both calibration regimes, an observed gain of 3.2 percentage points pooled whose per-regime confidence intervals include zero. The per-class keepout holds its coverage near the target on held-out recordings.
bullets: Problem: Inaccurate range maps and planner buffers can make narrow passages impassable, while standard deployment does not ensure stopping before moving keepouts.
Method: Condition the conformal keepout margin on a label-free severity estimate and enforce a braking-distance constraint during planning and every control command.
Design: Use measured tracking residuals as the only additional margin and never modify the calibrated keepout.
Evaluation: Validate keepout coverage on ground-robot smoke recordings and test closed-loop navigation in simulated quadrotor flights through a foggy tunnel.

Result and scope: The system reduced keepout entries and reached numerically more goals than the standard deployment; the pooled gain was 3.2 percentage points, but per-regime confidence intervals included zero.

papers.abstract: Humanoids and other legged robots operating in complex environments must remember information that leaves their field of view and only becomes relevant much later. Reinforcement learning policies address this using memory networks such as LSTMs that are trained end-to-end with the policy to memorize such task-relevant aspects. Yet, such architectures often fail to preserve sufficient information over long horizons. In this work, we propose a network architecture based on Hadamard memory that specifically targets robot navigation. Our Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) enables RL agents to store generic task-relevant information at specific, position-based memory cells, enabling flexible and spatially grounded memorization. We evaluate LSMM on the task of autonomous maze exploration, where it matches the maze coverage of strong recurrent and finite-history baselines while being the only architecture that remembers the maze layout, reducing the reconstruction error threefold.
authors: Leon Magnus, Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Long-horizon navigation requires remembering information beyond the robot’s current field of view.
The proposed Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) stores task-relevant information in position-based memory cells.
LSMM is evaluated for autonomous maze exploration against recurrent and finite-history baselines.
It matches baseline maze coverage and is the only evaluated architecture to remember maze layout, reducing reconstruction error threefold.

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time 3D object detection based on LiDAR and camera data is critical for safety in autonomous driving, where systems must accurately perceive their surroundings with minimal latency. Many state-of-the-art systems achieve high-quality detection results but fail to meet real-time constraints, limiting their practical use. To address this challenge, we propose FastBEVFusion, a simple, fast, and robust fusion system for 3D object detection. Based on modality-specific features, FastBEVFusion projects these features into semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces, without relying on a computationally intensive and potentially error-prone depth estimation. Given these BEV spaces, we propose a light-weight, soft, and dynamic fusion module based on cross-attention, which adapts dynamically to the scene context and enables feature fusion across the entire BEV spaces. Experiments on the complex nuScenes dataset show that FastBEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems, and achieves over 50 FPS without deployment libraries. Additionally, our system shows strong robustness to calibration errors, making FastBEVFusion a powerful 3D object detection system for real-world applications.
authors: Tom Sanitz, Emre G\"ulsoylu, Simone Frintrop, Christian Wilms
bullets: Targets the latency and reliability challenges of real-time multimodal 3D detection for autonomous driving.
Projects modality-specific features into semi-aligned BEV spaces without computationally expensive depth estimation.
Uses lightweight cross-attention for scene-adaptive fusion across the full BEV representation.
Evaluated on nuScenes, it outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems and exceeds 50 FPS without deployment libraries.
Shows strong robustness to calibration errors, supporting practical real-world use.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our FastBEVFusion. Multi-view image data is encoded and projected into an image BEV space using a uniform depth distribution to ensure low latency (color-coded in shades of green for different views). During training, an additional 2D object detection head is added. In parallel, the LiDAR point cloud is encoded into a LiDAR BEV space. The semi-aligned BEV spaces are then fused in our light-weight fusion module using on a single attention block exploiting the semi-aligned nature of the BEV spaces (see Fig. 3 for details). Based on the resulting fused BEV space, a detection head generates multi-modal 3D object detections.

Fig. 1. Results of real-time capable 3D object detection methods on the nuScenes dataset. Here, the two versions of our proposed FastBEVFusion based on different backbones offer the best detection quality and latency. Table I presents detailed results. Some latencies are estimated (see Sec. IV).

Fig. 4. Qualitative results of TransFusion-L [1] and our FastBEVFusion in three scenes of the nuScenes dataset. Only one of six views per scene is presented for brevity. Detected objects are color-coded by predicted classes: blue (pedestrians), orange (cars), and red (trucks).

Fig. 3. Detailed view of our light-weight fusion module based on a single multi-head attention block. The modality-specific BEV spaces are encoded and downsampled, before being tokenized and enriched with positional encodings. Subsequently, one multi-head attention layer is applied with tokens from image features as keys/values and tokens from LiDAR features as queries to efficiently learning a soft and dynamic fusion exploiting the semi-aligned nature of the features. Finally, an MLP is applied and a skip connection from the original LiDAR BEV space is added, before upsampling the features, yielding the fused BEV space. Note that we omit typical normalization steps in Transformers for brevity.

papers.abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.
authors: Sahar Nasirihaghighi, Tianyuan Wang, Kenan Niu, Stefano Stramigioli
bullets: Addresses the need for structured, continuous coronary-scene understanding beyond separate vessel segmentation or device localization.
Uses simulated fluoroscopy generated from 3D coronary CT angiography, including vessels, guidewires, stenoses, and varied geometries.
Jointly predicts vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip location, and stenosis location from a single X-ray frame.
Transforms predictions into a vascular graph with centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and angles.
Generates an interpretable roadmap from a selected graph root to the target lesion; evaluation is demonstrated in simulation.

The predicted vasculature is converted into a structured centerline graph and combined with the predicted stenosis target to generate a navigation-oriented roadmap.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation (ImageNav) requires an agent to reach a location specified by a goal image in an unknown environment. For drones, this task demands exploration, goal- directed navigation, and collision avoidance under limited onboard computing resources. Existing aerial ImageNav methods are built on single-view observations, requiring additional rotation and exploration to search for goal-relevant cues outside the field of view. In this paper, we present Omni-IGN, a fully onboard ImageNav system that integrates quad-fisheye perception, an attention-based reinforcement learning (RL) policy, and a collision-aware safety layer. The policy adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views to provide directional guidance for continuous navigation. The quad-fisheye RGB images support both ImageNav and obstacle avoidance without a dedicated depth sensor. On Habitat benchmarks, Omni-IGN achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines. Moreover, flight tests in IsaacSim validate the effectiveness of integrating learning-based depth estimation with the action safety layer for collision avoidance. Finally, real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without any fine-tuning or external localization. The code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zichen Yan, Rui Huang, Shenao Wang, Yucong Wang, Nuthasith Gerdpratoom, Lin Zhao

Demonstrates collision avoidance in IsaacSim and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in real-world experiments.

papers.abstract: Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution and subsequent replanning.
authors: Shuo Pei, Bosun Liang, Saihui Zha, Chen Sun, Huachun Tan, Yong Wang
bullets: Identifies a sample-to-execution gap: better generated proposals can still lead to worse committed actions.
Combines intent-guided diffusion proposals with execution-grounded candidate selection.
Feeds the committed trajectory back into subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics.
Reports leading closed-loop performance across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, including an average score of 85.62 and 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM.
Counterfactual and prefix analyses indicate more reliable conversion of strong candidates into executed decisions.

Strengthening proposals alone may raise the available-candidate ceiling while widening candidate-publication regret. ExecDiffuser connects proposal learning and trajectory publication through shared execution semantics: IGD improves candidate availability, while recurrent EGS commits one trajectory to control and returns it to the next planning cycle.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an approach to achieve side-by-side autonomous motion with a pair of personal mobility vehicles (PMVs). Given a global path, two PMVs plan cooperatively so as to hold a social formation that lets the passengers hold a conversation, while keeping the ride safe and smooth. Each vehicle runs its own sampling-based model-predictive planner; the planners exchange nothing but the odometry each vehicle could observe of the other, and the joint decision is expressed as a pair of utility matrices over pairs of candidate trajectories, resolved by a common rule. The behavioural parameters are fitted by inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by ten pairs of people in human-driven PMVs in an indoor environment, and the lanes the pair can use are derived offline from the corridor itself rather than fixed by hand. A safety layer the cost cannot override executes a move only if the vehicle can still brake clear, measured from its whole body, and a vehicle that is stuck reverses along its own path and continues. In closed-loop simulation over 24 runs in the conditions the drivers were recorded in and 24 in four generated obstacle layouts, no vehicle entered a wall or a cone. The pair holds conversational formation for 60.5 and 68.9 percent of the time among obstacles (anticlockwise and clockwise) and 81.2 and 91.5 percent in a clear aisle, against the drivers' 34.0 and 36.0 percent, and 52.9 and 56.0 percent, and it matches their speed. It keeps one lateral formation where the drivers alternated between a close diagonal and a wide abreast one, and it varies far less. Experimental results are based on a differential drive kinematic simulator running on ROS 2.
bullets: Uses inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by 10 human pairs to fit cooperative behavioral parameters.
Each vehicle runs a sampling-based model-predictive planner and exchanges only observable odometry with its partner.
A common utility-matrix rule coordinates trajectory choices, while corridor-derived lanes and a non-overridable braking-based safety layer support navigation.
In simulation, no vehicle collided with walls or cones across 48 closed-loop runs, and conversational formation was maintained more often than by human drivers.
The system matched driver speed but used a more consistent lateral formation; evaluation was limited to a differential-drive kinematic simulator in ROS 2.

papers.abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Ziang Guo, Didar Seyidov, Yixiao Zhou, Xuefeng Zhang, Ali Alridha Abdulkarim, Chen Min, Zufeng Zhang, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Addresses cascading map degradation caused by absorbing monocular tracking errors into the map.
Uses chunk-level streaming spatial geometry as a metric prior to supervise both tracking and mapping.
Introduces a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel that models viewpoint-dependent information.
Jointly optimizes geometry and poses to produce globally consistent maps and trajectories.
Outperforms per-frame association baselines on KITTI and Waymo Open datasets.

The chunk fusion is solved over the spatial geometry and poses via a global joint graph.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining long-range navigation with precision vertical landing under nonlinear dynamics and uncertainty.
Uses a three-stage curriculum, critic warm-up, rehearsal to limit catastrophic forgetting, and observations containing a full 3×3 rotation matrix.
Introduces a bounded, computationally simpler reward function whose progress term tracks cumulative distance closed.
Under the reported evaluation, the policy achieved 99.98% success versus 68.31% for the baseline.
The proposed policy retained 69.1% initial fuel and had 7.07 units mean final pad-distance, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline.

papers.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
bullets: Direct-policy world action models typically need tens of denoising steps, limiting real-time deployment.
OSWAM uses imagination tokens to provide physical priors and action-conditioned representations at diffusion initialization.
Privileged information distillation with future conditioning improves future-aware action generation.
Experiments report comparable or better performance than multi-step direct-policy and Joint-WAM baselines, with about 3× speedup and latency as low as 40 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.
The abstract evaluates autonomous driving and embodied control, without specifying broader domains or limitations.

papers.abstract: Robotic missions involving spatially distributed tasks often require jointly selecting rewarding locations and planning feasible motions under limited travel budgets. This paper proposes Reward-Guided RRT*, a new sampling-based framework that constructs a budget-feasible mission through a sequence of locally joint task-selection-and-motion-planning stages, evaluated directly in the continuous state space, without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph. The method incrementally builds a mission using reward-guided RRT* searches, while a return-feasibility procedure ensures that each selected task can be visited without violating the mission budget. Experiments with increasing obstacle complexity and number of tasks show solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* while requiring substantially fewer sampled states. We also extend the framework to Dubins steering and evaluate it in CoppeliaSim with a scaled car-like robotic platform, demonstrating its ability to incorporate vehicle kinematic constraints.
bullets: Builds missions incrementally through locally joint task-selection and motion-planning stages.
Uses reward-guided RRT* without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph.
Applies return-feasibility checks to ensure selected tasks remain within the mission budget.
Achieves solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* with substantially fewer sampled states in experiments.
Extends to Dubins steering and demonstrates operation with a car-like robot in CoppeliaSim.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.
bullets: A matched 12-candidate tuning protocol changed the baseline RMSE ranking, moving BL-SMC from last to first; this ordering persisted on fresh realizations and with 48 candidates.
Reference preview substantially improved MPC tracking and eliminated fallback activity on the figure-eight task.
On abrupt steps, performance depended on the interaction among fallback policy, actuator prediction, and actuator authority.
Measured command delays caused most or all tested nominal MPC configurations to miss deadlines, while a 100-iteration solver cap removed deadline misses in tested profiles.
The study recommends reporting tracking accuracy alongside tuning effort, completion/failure rates, fallback activity, input variation, and timing.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.
bullets: Targets inefficient exploration in sampling-based drone planning for complex 3D environments.
Converts natural-language instructions into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints.
Uses command-aligned subset sampling to structure exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness.
Simulations produce collision-free, consistent trajectories with reduced sampling effort versus uniform RRT-based planners.

papers.abstract: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds have matured into a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC, but they remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, we contribute a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators through a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of the software stack we build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, and a controller that exploits these added degrees of freedom, letting classical optimal controllers and learned policies be swapped on the same hardware without modification. We validate the integrated system, PINGU, across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The results show that these additions extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of thruster-only planar spacecraft testbeds for inertia-coupled manipulation and contact-rich operations.
Integrates a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms with interchangeable end-effectors through a unified ROS 2 interface.
Provides a reinforcement-learning environment and digital twin supporting interchangeable classical optimal controllers and learned policies.
Validates the system on navigation, disturbance rejection, momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking tasks.
Demonstrates an ATMOS-class emulator extended into the contact-rich regime on a single reproducible platform.

The control domain (Battery 1, 22.2 V nominal, regulated) supplies the flight controller, compute, and solenoid loads. Each instance contains a full PINGU model (air-bearing platform with two LEVION arms) and two UR10 manipulator mounted to the ceiling and wall rails, replicating the physical laboratory layout. Massively parallel rollouts with domain randomization enable the sim-to-real transfer results reported in Section IV.

The configurations are held fixed during each run and are not part of the controller’s action space; they serve as a structured way to stress-test controller robustness across different inertial regimes.

The symmetric bilateral mounting allows the arms to reconfigure the platform’s effective inertia distribution on-the-fly.

papers.title: PINGU: Extending Air-Bearing Spacecraft Emulators with Open-Source Actuators and Learned Control for Contact-Rich Proximity Operations
papers.tldr: PINGU upgrades an open-source air-bearing spacecraft emulator with reaction-wheel and force-sensing arm actuators, enabling reproducible contact-rich proximity-operation experiments with both classical and learned control.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving maps current observations directly to future trajectories, yet those trajectories must remain valid as the scene evolves. Future state modeling aims to address this temporal mismatch, but general representations often contain information unrelated to ego planning and affect trajectory generation only through auxiliary supervision, static conditioning, or proposal evaluation. We propose FeasibleFlow, a one-step end-to-end generative framework that jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories. Our Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow uses the pathwise Jacobian-vector product in the MeanFlow identity to incorporate field evolution into trajectory transport. Because safety feedback is sparser than progress feedback, we further introduce the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) and Pareto-ReinFlow to balance safety and progress in candidate selection and generation, respectively. Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate the strong performance of FeasibleFlow and validate both the joint transport of feasibility and trajectories and the proposed safety-first mechanisms.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static observations and trajectories that must remain valid as scenes evolve.
Introduces Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow to couple feasibility-field evolution with trajectory transport via a pathwise Jacobian-vector product.
Uses Anchor-relative ranker and Pareto-ReinFlow to prioritize sparse safety feedback while balancing safety and progress.
NAVSIM experiments demonstrate strong performance and support the value of joint feasibility–trajectory transport and safety-first mechanisms.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture and training pipeline of FeasibleFlow. (a) During supervised training, a DeepSets encoder and implicit decoder learn the feasibility field from logged configuration labels. Field and action states are transported by the Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow, and the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) selects the final candidate through its Imitation ranker and Outcome ranker. (b) Pareto-ReinFlow uses the frozen ranker to select a reference trajectory, evaluates exploratory trajectories by their relative safety and progress, and updates only the online action MeanFlow.

Fig. 1. Motivation and key mechanism of FeasibleFlow. A trajectoryonly generator leaves future feasibility implicit. FeasibleFlow instead jointly transports a graded configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego actions. The evolving field enters action transport through the cross-JVP term of the Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow, while inference remains a single transport step.

Fig. 4. Qualitative comparison with MeanFuser [14]. The top and bottom rows show off-road and collision cases, respectively. From left to right, each row presents the front-camera image, the MeanFuser result, and the FeasibleFlow result. Red circles mark the critical regions.

Fig. 3. Visualization of configuration-space feasibility. From left to right: the front-camera image, multimodal trajectory candidates with the selected plan, and the predicted feasibility field. Brighter regions in the heatmap indicate higher predicted feasibility. The field view overlays the exact configuration-space boundary, selected and ground-truth trajectories.

papers.abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$
bullets: Introduces 16 database–query datasets from terrestrial Space Analog Domains, covering environmental, viewpoint, and illumination variation.
Defines matches by whether a relative pose estimator can produce a useful pose for downstream SLAM, rather than by fixed pose thresholds.
Provides ground-truth matrices derived from an ensemble of state-of-the-art relative pose estimators.
Evaluates nine state-of-the-art VPR methods and finds substantial room for improvement.
Offers a pre-release dataset and evaluation resources via GitHub.

Based on pose thresholding or frustum overlap these images should match. papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.
authors: Khaled M. Seyam (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Julian Wiederer (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Samar Fathalah (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Markus Braun (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Bin Yang (University of Stuttgart, Germany)
bullets: NeuroNCAP analysis attributes 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions to planning failures rather than perception.
The method attacks each planner through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its planning head, avoiding video rendering during search.
Automated quality-diversity search generates 50 attack scenes per planner, each paired with a safe escape trajectory for fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning roughly halves collision rates for SparseDrive and DiffusionDrive on NeuroNCAP, from 28.0% to 12.2% and 37.5% to 19.2%, respectively.
Cross-planner transfer is limited, indicating that targeting the specific planner is important; scope is demonstrated on two planners and NeuroNCAP.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Method. (A) Only the adapter Aθ trains; the planner’s own planning head fhead is copied and frozen, so gradients through π̂ point at the planner’s failure modes. (B) Adversary controls (a, δ) are optimized against the collision objective J through the surrogate, and a quality-diversity grid keeps the attack closest to the ego per cell, so attack types are found rather than specified. (C) The escape is solved by geometry with the attacker held fixed, and scenes with no valid escape are rejected. (D) Surviving scenes are rendered and only parameters inside the planning head of π are updated.

Fig. 1. Model-aware adversarial fine-tuning. We distill an end-to-end planner into a differentiable surrogate, optimize adversarial scenarios against it, and render them to fine-tune that planner. The renderer never enters the optimization loop. Bottom: closed-loop collision rate on NeuroNCAP. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself.

Fig. 4. Attacks discovered against each planner differ. Those against DiffusionDrive are predominantly cut-ins and almost never head-on threats, while those against SparseDrive also include head-on and front-brake attacks.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses safety-critical scene generation and fine-tuning for end-to-end driving planners, directly relevant to learned robot navigation and policy learning.
papers.title: Model-Aware Generation of Safety-Critical Scenes for Robust End-to-End Driving via Distilled Planner Surrogates
papers.tldr: A planner-specific, model-aware scene-generation framework uses distilled BEV planner surrogates to create safety-critical training scenes that substantially reduce collisions while preserving normal driving.

papers.abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Hanchao Leng, JiaHui Huang, Hanbing Li, Jingwei Zhao, Kuiyuan Yang, Chen Gao, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses information loss and cross-modal inconsistency caused by modeling driving modalities separately.
Encodes appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories into a shared continuous latent.
Uses a frozen tokenizer with a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents.
On NAVSIM, the unified design improves future prediction and planning while reducing downstream computational cost.
With reinforcement-learning post-training, DriveUniWAM reaches a PDMS of 91.54 and state-of-the-art performance among evaluated WAM planners.

figures.caption: Figure 2: DriveUniTok architecture. (a) Encoder. RGB, projected depth, and ego pose are fused into S shared queries, whose T per-frame states are compressed into one latent. (b) Decoder. The latent is expanded back to T frame positions, and each target is read out through its own set of mask tokens, including a training-only semantic branch. Snowflakes mark frozen components, and all remaining modules are trained.

Figure 1: Comparison of latent representations for world-action modeling. (a) BEV tokenizers fuse RGB and LiDAR into a visual latent, while (b) Occupancy tokenizers represent the scene with an occupancy latent; both keep ego motion separate. (c) Modality-specific tokenizers encode RGB, LiDAR, and ego motion into separate streams. (d) DriveUniTok jointly encodes RGB, LiDAR-derived geometry, and ego motion into one unified latent.

Figure 3: Training and policy optimization with DriveUniWAM. (a) Supervised training. DriveUniWAM forecasts the future latents with flow matching. (b) Reinforcement learning. Per scene, a group of sampled futures is decoded into trajectories and scored by the NAVSIM PDM reward, whose relative advantages drive the Flow-GRPO update. DriveUniTok stays frozen in both stages.

papers.abstract: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1--31.2\% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.

papers.abstract: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. The source code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
authors: Hyunwoong Bae, Jisu Han, Jiyeon Choi, Dohoon Kim, Taesup Moon

papers.abstract: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons's hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29 m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.

papers.abstract: Floor traction influences wheel-slip behavior, dead-reckoning accuracy, and the navigation performance of wheeled mobile robots that rely on wheel odometry. As these robots become increasingly common in GNSS-denied indoor environments, including automated manufacturing and retail facilities, their onboard measurements could also be used to characterize floor conditions and improve localization. In this study, a skid-steer robot was driven over five floor surfaces with distinct traction characteristics using commanded velocity profiles designed to induce wheel slip through repeated acceleration and direction reversal. Differences between the body velocity estimated from inertial sensing and the velocity obtained from wheel odometry were evaluated using the integrated relative-velocity error, phase-derived wheel-to-body response delay, and velocity-reversal response delay. Welch power spectral density analysis was additionally applied to characterize the frequency distribution of the velocity mismatch during positive and negative acceleration. Band-integrated spectral power, spectral centroid, and spectral decay rate were extracted from each recording and evaluated using linear discriminant analysis and multiclass classification. The response-delay measurements produced consistent surface-dependent trends, with the longest delays observed on soap and the shortest delays observed on carpet. The spectral features also provided clear separation among the tested surfaces, achieving a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These results demonstrate that both the magnitude and frequency domain characteristics of wheel-to-body velocity mismatch contain useful information about tire-surface interactions. Such information could support surface recognition and the development of slip-aware wheel-odometry weighting within robot state-estimation frameworks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating in dynamic, challenging conditions such as intersections and roundabouts must guarantee collision avoidance under uncertainty while maintaining real-time feasibility. Most existing planners struggle to simultaneously guarantee both requirements. Chance-constrained formulations embed safety constraints directly in the optimization but become infeasible as uncertainty compounds; deterministic planners provide feasible solutions but fail to address the uncertainty that causes collisions; end-to-end learned policies provide neither guarantee in an interpretable form. We present a modular perception-prediction-planning pipeline that closes this gap by propagating uncertainty as structured, interpretable quantities across module boundaries. Rather than embedding probabilistic risk directly in the optimization, our pipeline resolves collision probabilities upstream and constructs convex safe sets within which the planner provides a guaranteed feasible solution at every cycle -- decoupling the safety guarantee from solver feasibility. Across Monte Carlo trials in a four-way unsignalized intersection, our pipeline achieves 0% collisions and 0% solver infeasibility at 12.7ms per cycle, compared to 36% and 10% collision rates for deterministic and chance-constrained baselines respectively. The ablation study confirms the necessity of each uncertainty source and the hardware deployment on Clearpath Jackal UGVs validates the pipeline's real-time viability on physical platforms.
authors: Doris Xu, Jin Hyun Park, Guadalupe Alvarado Fernandez, Adhyan Prasad, Mark Campbell
bullets: Targets safe, feasible autonomous driving in uncertain dynamic scenarios such as intersections and roundabouts.
Propagates structured uncertainty through modular perception, prediction, and planning components.
Resolves collision probabilities upstream and builds convex safe sets for a guaranteed feasible planner solution each cycle.
In four-way unsignalized-intersection Monte Carlo trials, it reported 0% collisions, 0% solver infeasibility, and 12.7 ms per cycle.
Ablations and Clearpath Jackal UGV deployment support the importance of the uncertainty sources and real-time physical viability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Pipeline Architecture Overview: The IMM estimates the agent’s intent probabilities and states. The forecaster produces the forecasted trajectories. The collision detector combines these forecasted trajectories with the ego localizer’s state estimates to compute per-intent collision probabilities. The decision maker converts these probabilities into a convex safe set, within which the flat MPC plans and the CBF safety filter enforces forward invariance.

(a) The IMM produces per-intent mode probabilities µj ; the forecaster propagates each into a trajectory (blue) with compounded covariance ellipses. (b) The collision detector finds the closest OBB approach n∗ (blue markers) along each forecast. (c) Combined covariance Σ is projected onto the separation direction to yield P j col analytically. (d) The decision maker sweeps the agent’s OBB along the most likely forecast to form the unsafe region U and constructs the convex safe set S and determines the intermediate goal pose (shown as a red star) for the downstream planner and safety filter.

Fig. 4. Snapshots of three experiment scenarios at three different times: t0 is the start time, t1 is the time of highest collision probability, and t2 is the time when the unsafe set no longer intersects with the lane. papers.abstract: In a decentralized multi-robot team under partial observability, the fact that decides a robot's next action is often visible only to a teammate. Existing decentralized methods communicate kinematic information, such as position or planned trajectory, which cannot convey what the teammate perceives. Learned communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) can carry perceptual content, but the resulting messages are task-coupled and opaque. We propose Latent Telepathy. Each robot broadcasts the perceptual latent vector it already computes for its own use, the output of an encoder trained with a self-supervised joint-embedding predictive objective, frozen, and shared across the team. A teammate learns to act on it from task reward alone. Because the encoder already runs for perception, the message costs no additional computation and a single compact vector of bandwidth. Because the encoder is frozen before any policy is trained, the message means the same thing to every robot, and the receiving robot is never told what it means. We evaluate Latent Telepathy with a content-controlled protocol in which bandwidth, latency, topology and receiver are held fixed and only the message content varies. Broadcasting the latent lets a navigator avoid an occluded hazard in 99.7% of episodes, matching a noiseless hand-designed message. Position and trajectory messages remain at chance, and the raw camera image, 186 times wider, is less reliable than the compressed latent. The result holds from a discrete gridworld to rendered pixels under continuous velocity control, and the encoder decodes the hazard from a physical robot's camera in 102 of 102 live decisions. We also identify a requirement for porting MARL communication results to continuous control, that the decision a message informs must remain reachable by exploration, and show how to restore it.
bullets: Addresses partial observability where critical perceptual information is visible only to another robot.
Broadcasts each robot’s existing frozen perceptual latent, avoiding extra computation and using one compact message vector.
The shared encoder gives messages consistent meaning across robots while receivers learn to use them from task reward alone.
Latent messages enabled hazard avoidance in 99.7% of episodes, matched a noiseless hand-designed signal, and outperformed position, trajectory, and raw-image messages.
Results span gridworld, rendered pixels with continuous control, and 102/102 live physical-robot decisions; successful transfer requires the informed action to remain reachable through exploration.

papers.abstract: Self-play in high-throughput simulators yields driving policies with robust closed-loop performance, but improvement per unit of simulation diminishes as training scales. Policies learn to handle common situations early, while further rollouts repeatedly encounter unresolved failures. Post-training offers an opportunity to target these failures, but existing methods primarily evaluate alternative actions or continuations at visited states, although successful recovery may require changing driving style earlier. We propose CounterPlay, a counterfactual self-play post-training approach that backtracks from failed tasks and retries them under alternate driving styles. CounterPlay rests on three key components. First, failure-driven backtracking uses the policy's value estimates to select an earlier stored state from which to retry the task. Second, reward conditioning enables a single policy to retry the task from this state using candidate styles ranging from cautious to aggressive. Third, CounterPlay retains task-completing retries only if no other vehicle incurs a new or earlier collision or off-road event relative to the factual branch. Retries that pass verification with fresh randomness are then distilled into the policy under its deployment condition. On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both the Interactive and Random splits across all eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions, which is just 1% of the anchor's 100B self-play training budget. Improvements over the anchor hold across all three evaluated driving styles. CounterPlay resolves a substantial fraction of the anchor's timeout cases on BehaviorBench and achieves a balance between task completion and safety that neither continued self-play nor adopting a more aggressive driving style attains.
bullets: Targets diminishing self-play gains by focusing on unresolved failures rather than repeatedly sampling common situations.
Backtracks from failures to an earlier state selected using value estimates, then retries with styles from cautious to aggressive via reward conditioning.
Keeps only verified retries that complete the task without introducing earlier or additional collisions or off-road events.
Distills successful retries into the policy under its normal deployment condition.
On BehaviorBench, reaches state-of-the-art scores across eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions—1% of the anchor’s 100B self-play budget—and resolves many timeout cases.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CounterPlay. Based on a pretrained self-play anchor policy, Stage 1 uses critic estimates recorded along the failed trajectory to select an earlier root. Stage 2 then restores this state and simulates a factual branch under the original reward condition and retries under the candidate profiles. Stage 3 filters and ranks retries using task completion and other-vehicle outcomes relative to the factual branch. It then reruns the factual and selected branches with fresh shared random draws to verify the recovery. Stage 4 distills the verified retry into the policy under the deployment condition.

Fig. 3. Qualitative results. Each pair compares the anchor (left) and CounterPlay (right) in the same scene and traffic regime. Ego trajectories are colored by elapsed time in seconds. Grey arrows show other road users’ motion. Open boxes mark ego starts and stars mark goals. Red crosses mark collisions. Circles and triangles mark timeouts and off-road events, respectively.

Fig. 1. The self-play policy repeatedly waits for a gap and times out. Re-sampling the same driving style from a late state fails to recover the task. CounterPlay backtracks to an earlier root and explores alternative driving styles. An aggressive retry completes the task, passes verification with fresh randomness, and is distilled under the deployment condition.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.
Reports higher success and modestly better path efficiency than WMNav on HM3D v0.1 and MP3D.
On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.

papers.abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multimodal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird's eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
authors: Samuel Triest, Amirreza Shaban, David D. Fan, Wenshan Wang, Sebastian Scherer
bullets: Addresses robust traversability estimation under limited sensing, complex terrain, and high-speed motion.
Builds a geometric-semantic voxel map from onboard multimodal sensors using visual foundation models.
Jointly predicts BEV geometry, semantics, speed, and cost with annotation-free self-supervised learning, including map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning.
Ablations show that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting improve planning quality, with their combination needed for state-of-the-art off-road planning.
Real-world experiments report 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal when combining inpainting with uncertainty-based risk estimation.

Fig. 5. Two scenarios from the test set. Cost and speed maps are cropped and enlarged to highlight regions of interest.
