papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.

papers.abstract: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
authors: Kaibo Yang, Xingyu Wu, Enze Zhu, Yajie Chai, Xuyang Li, Jiahui Cui, Xiaoxuan Liu, Lei Wang, Zhan Chen

papers.abstract: Candidate-based end-to-end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene-relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty. To address these challenges, we introduce Expand-and-Prune, a test-time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters. The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates. Across four heterogeneous candidate-based planners and four benchmarks, Expand-and-Prune consistently improves planning performance. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.2 to 75.9, while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out-of-distribution scenarios. Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent-guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate-space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner. The code is available at https://github.com/iis-esslingen/Expand-and-Prune.

papers.abstract: Achieving precise terminal position and heading alignment remains a significant challenge for learning-based mobile robot control. Recent vision-based learning methods have shown promise for precise target-relative control and generalization to unseen environments with pretrained visual encoders, but general-purpose visual representations are not specifically designed to capture the fine-grained spatial differences between current and goal views required for precise control, and real-world demonstrations combining millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that leverages a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. Rather than using the final relative-pose estimate, GR-VIP conditions action prediction on the dense relational features produced before pose regression, preserving fine-grained cross-view information for learning corrective actions from demonstrations. We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world docking task and demonstrate high docking success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy in both the training and unseen environments, without additional training for transfer. Furthermore, supplementary experiments illustrate the policy's ability to align with non-docking targets and complete docking under a tested low-light condition.

Also demonstrates alignment to non-docking targets and docking under a tested low-light condition.

papers.abstract: A robot swarm covers a building faster with more robots, but the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically visited. We target the amount of an unknown building a decentralized swarm knows at each instant, ahead of physical coverage. SenseSwarm serves a lightweight learned map predictor on the swarm's shared occupancy map and folds the predicted structure back into a stigmergic guidance field. Its 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on the swarm's own multi-front observations, which we show is necessary: a single-robot predictor collapses on such views. We build a benchmark of twelve real building floors from HouseExpo, HKUST, and KTH, up to 24,000 square meters, and run 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes 32 to 512, and three seeds. On physical coverage the swarm is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, as expected. On map reconstruction, every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and SenseSwarm holds an equal-time area lead of about 670 square meters, up to 1,359. Folding the prediction into the shared field matters: the same predictor applied per robot matches our speed but suffers a 6.9 times higher inter-robot contact rate at 512 robots. The prediction is computed once per shared map, so its cost stayed flat from 32 to 512 robots.
authors: Haohua Que, Haojia Gao, Mingkai Liu, Hoiian Au, Qian Zhang, Jiayue Xie, Yule Cai, Bokui Chen, Xueqian Wang, Fei Qiao
bullets: Targets earlier knowledge of unknown building structure, beyond physical exploration coverage.

papers.abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle's dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle's dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure. At each step, we query the bird's-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset's most difficult scenarios. On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ($\geq$10 m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics .
authors: Micah Nye, Samuel Triest, Matthew Sivaprakasam, Isaiah Adu, Sebastian Scherer, Wenshan Wang
bullets: Off-road terrain interactions create complex dynamics that simplistic perception conditioning may miss.

papers.abstract: GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance (Fig. 1). Future research may focus on improving 1) the generality of ICL 2) cost and execution time, 3) physical-state verification, 4) recovery from irreversible failures, and 5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. We identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner (i.e., GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller (e.g., {\pi}0.5) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for ICL are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate. Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence.

Key open challenges include generalizable in-context learning, execution cost and time, state verification, recovery from irreversible failures, and preserving progress over long horizons.

papers.abstract: Tiny robots have limited computation and memory, yet visual navigation systems often maintain more state than a task requires. We ask whether persistent memory can instead be shaped by the task. We present \textbf{RingNav}, a \(10.6\)k--parameter visual heading estimator that constrains its memory to the circular manifold \(S^1\). RingNav learns only the turn between consecutive images, while heading is composed directly on the circle. On the TartanAir Visual SLAM Challenge, RingNav reduces mean absolute turn error by \(27\%\) and accumulated heading error over $4$ sec by \(15\%\) relative to a similarly sized learned-memory model. The structured update also gives exactly zero turn for identical frames and exact cancellation under sequence reversal. Without fine-tuning, RingNav transfers to real-world drone experiments and continues estimating heading under severe visual degradation. RingNav runs at $27.3$Hz on Raspberry Pi Zero 2W and can be deployed on an ultra-low power GAP8 processor at $33.4$Hz.

papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a critical component of autonomous navigation in unstructured environments, where complex and uncertain robot-terrain interactions pose significant challenges such as traction loss and dynamic instability. Despite recent progress in learning-based traversability prediction, these methods often fail to adapt to novel terrains. Even when adaptation is achieved, retaining experience from previously trained environments remains a challenge, a problem known as catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose a continual learning framework for traversability prediction that incrementally adapts to new terrains using a generative experience recall model. A key virtue of the proposed framework is two folds: i) retain prior experience without storing past data; and ii) incorporate the uncertainty of the generated samples from the recall model, enabling uncertainty-aware adaptation. Real-world experiments with a skid-steering robot validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, demonstrating its ability to adapt across a series of diverse environments while mitigating catastrophic forgetting.
bullets: Addresses poor adaptation to novel terrains and catastrophic forgetting in traversability prediction.
Incrementally adapts the model using a generative experience recall model without storing past data.
Uses uncertainty estimates from recalled samples to guide adaptation.
Real-world skid-steering robot experiments show adaptation across diverse environments while mitigating forgetting.

papers.abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.
bullets: Plans parabolic hops and diverts to safe landing sites when nominal waypoints are unsafe or unreachable.
Uses semantic segmentation to detect obstacles and rapidly computes reachable terrain.
Applies model predictive control (MPC) to track hop trajectories toward safe landing sites.
High-fidelity lunar simulations show safe, fuel-efficient trajectories that MPC tracks rapidly with low error.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The drone hops between global waypoints. In-flight, when the drone can see its next waypoint, it identifies unsafe obstacles near the waypoint using semantic segmentation. It also calculates the reachable set of landing sites from a starting point a few seconds in the future along the tracked launch trajectory. The nominal landing site is unsafe, so the drone starts calculating the optimal descent trajectory to the nearest safe and reachable landing site. A few seconds in the future, when the descent trajectory is calculated, the drone diverts to its new landing site. Closer to the ground, it checks for smaller obstacles that the semantic segmentation model may have missed from its high vantage point. It identifies a rock at its new landing site and adjusts the remaining descent trajectory to divert to a safe final landing position.

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.
authors: Siwei Cai, Yuwei Wu, Vijay Kumar, Lifeng Zhou
bullets: Addresses the human-aware safety gap: pedestrians, vehicles, and walls receive different clearance requirements instead of being treated as generic occupied geometry.
Fuses BLIP-based captioning and text-conditioned segmentation with depth to localize obstacles in 3D.
Uses a lightweight Qwen-2.5-0.5B LLM with retrieval grounding and grammar-constrained JSON outputs; category-level verdicts are cached and detections persist through occlusions.
Runs perception at 10 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, with fallback LLM queries kept off the control-critical path.
In Gazebo, collision events decrease by roughly 3×, while semantic landing success among moving actors increases from 34% to 96%; small-object perception at range remains limited.

papers.abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
authors: Danqi Zhao, Keyu Chen, Wenchao Sun, Minglei Huang, Jianhe Zhang, Yan Zhu, Hao Cheng, Zifan Cao, Sifa Zheng
bullets: Problem: Different downstream controllers can execute the same plan differently, causing a gap between imagined and actual outcomes.
Naively substituting predicted or observed execution trajectories improves fidelity but does not reliably improve planning decisions.
Method: Infer controller-specific execution characteristics from planned–executed trajectory pairs and adapt the planner’s native ego latent rollout.
The world model, planner, and reward head remain frozen; the original planned trajectory is preserved.
On NAVSIM, the method consistently improves planning across unseen controllers and multiple frozen planners, especially in challenging driving scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of ExecutionBridge. (a) Controller Encoder. Given a support set of planned–executed trajectory pairs Sc, the Controller Encoder summarizes these observations into a compact controller representation ec that captures persistent controller-specific execution characteristics. An auxiliary execution decoder predicts the execution of a held-out query trajectory for training supervision and is discarded at deployment. (b) Controller-Conditioned Latent Bridge. For each candidate, the frozen world model first produces its native rollout from the original planned trajectory. Conditioned on ec, the Latent Bridge predicts a gated correction to the ego latent, which is bounded by a trust-region projection before being injected into the rollout. The resulting controller-conditioned rollout is evaluated by the unchanged reward model for candidate scoring.

Fig. 2. Planning–execution gap and motivation for ExecutionBridge. (a) The same planned trajectory can lead to different executions at deployment from those implicitly assumed by the frozen world model, causing its imagined future to deviate from the future actually encountered. (b) Directly substituting the planned trajectory with its executed counterpart improves execution fidelity, but introduces a plan–execution semantic mismatch: the executed trajectory can still be interpreted through the model’s implicit plan-to-motion mapping, and therefore does not necessarily improve candidate ranking. (c) ExecutionBridge instead retains the original planned trajectory as the conditioning input and uses controller-specific execution evidence to adapt the imagined future used for candidate evaluation.

Fig. 4. Representative planning results under the standard NAVSIM setting. Compared with frozen WoTE, ExecutionBridge yields trajectory selections that are better aligned with controller-dependent execution in representative collision and drivable-area failure cases.

Fig. 1. Evolution of end-to-end planning paradigms. Model-free planners predict or score trajectories directly from the current scene, without explicitly modeling their future consequences. Model-based planners additionally use a learned world model to imagine candidate-conditioned futures for trajectory evaluation. Conventional model-based planning typically assumes that candidate trajectories are executed according to the planto-motion relationship learned during training. Execution-adaptive modelbased planning further incorporates controller-specific information, allowing candidate futures to be evaluated under deployment-specific execution.

Fig. 6. Adaptation under representative controller styles. We show four representative controller configurations, including aggressive, conservative, steering-lag, and steering-gain behaviors. Controller-conditioned candidate evaluation consistently improves both PDM and Time to Collision (TTC) across these diverse controller styles. Examples on the right illustrate safetycritical cases in which accounting for controller-specific execution changes the selected trajectory and avoids failures under frozen evaluation.

Fig. 5. Planning under unseen controller shifts. Performance of the frozen planner and ExecutionBridge across ten unseen deployment controller configurations. (a) ExecutionBridge consistently improves PDMS across controller styles (mean: 87.98 → 88.59, +0.61). (b) It also improves TTC (mean: 94.53 → 94.86, +0.33). (c) The improvement is substantially larger on the low-score subset, where PDMS increases from 32.04 to 46.13 (+14.09). These results indicate that controller-conditioned adaptation is particularly beneficial in challenging driving scenes where candidate evaluation is more sensitive to execution differences.

Fig. 7. Execution fidelity does not imply decision fidelity. (a) Predicted and exact controller execution substantially reduce geometric execution error. (b–c) Nevertheless, candidate-ranking fidelity changes only marginally on the frozen-defined difficult-scene subset. (d) Direct execution substitution improves selected-candidate quality, but ExecutionBridge performs best by preserving the original plan and adapting its imagined future. Pairwise-oracle PDMS in (d) is a candidate-level diagnostic distinct from final navtest PDMS.

papers.abstract: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following. Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
authors: Yanci Wen, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Weixi Situ, Hanjing Ye, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses prolonged target loss caused by pedestrian occlusions in dynamic environments.
Uses language-guided perception to separate target and occluder observations, then combines visual history with ego-motion to estimate relative motion during partial visibility.
Predicts whether continued following will maintain occlusion and selectively triggers viewpoint-adjustment maneuvers through a recurrent controller.
Introduces OccEVT-Bench and expert demonstrations for closed-loop evaluation and training.
On the Risk split, improves success rate by 121.4% and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph--reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8\%, 60.8\%, and 27.4\%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4\%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.
authors: Zhao Yang, Zezhong Qian, Yinan Shi, Longjun Liu, Yawei Jueluo
bullets: Targets safer, rule-compliant, and more comfortable planning in complex multi-agent scenes.
Combines graph-aware importance weighting, time-indexed relational reward surrogates, and advantage-weighted diffusion training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to form a rollout–return–advantage–update loop without explicit likelihoods.
On nuPlan and interPlan, reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, while improving planning score by 3.4% over a diffusion-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Biological visual navigation achieves remarkable robustness at extremely low power, whereas frame-based robotic systems relying on artificial neural networks remain limited in both respects, particularly for energy-constrained micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) operating in complex environments. Inspired by the event-driven, sparse, and asynchronous principles of biological visual systems, neuromorphic sensing and computation provide a promising alternative for robust and energy-efficient navigation. In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for MAV visual navigation in complex environments by integrating neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors. The proposed method first extracts the environmental representation from event streams using a spiking perceptual representation module. This representation is fed into a spiking navigation module, where guidance learning and population coding enable efficient policy learning with few time steps. The navigation module then outputs a waypoint converted into executable trajectory points. Experiments show that the proposed neuromorphic method achieves navigation performance comparable to ANN-based methods while markedly reducing power consumption. The spiking perceptual module consumes only 19.57% of the power of its ANN counterpart, while the spiking navigation module deployed on Intel Loihi consumes only 12.37% of that required by its ANN counterpart running on NVIDIA Orin NX. Beyond prior neuromorphic systems focused mainly on relatively simple navigation subtasks, we demonstrate a complete neuromorphic visual navigation system spanning simulation and real-world deployment. Our results establish the feasibility of the neuromorphic paradigm for autonomous navigation and provide a bio-inspired pathway toward robust and low-power MAV navigation.
authors: Junjie Jiang, Ankang Zhou, Zheng Fang
bullets: Targets robust, energy-efficient navigation for micro aerial vehicles in complex environments.
Combines neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors.
Uses spiking perceptual representations, guidance learning, and population coding to produce executable waypoints.
Reports power use of 19.57% for the spiking perceptual module and 12.37% for the Loihi-based spiking navigation module relative to ANN counterparts.
Demonstrates a complete system in simulation and real-world deployment, extending beyond simpler neuromorphic navigation subtasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: End-to-end event-driven neuromorphic MAV navigation system. (A) Architecture of the proposed end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation system. The system comprises a spiking perceptual representation module and a spiking navigation policy module. The perceptual module converts event streams into compact, geometry-aware features, while the navigation policy module maps these visual features, together with the robot state and goal direction, to navigation actions. (B) Key hardware components of the neuromorphic system. The platform consists of a neuromorphic vision sensor (Prophesee EVK4), an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, an x86 host computer, a neuromorphic processor (Intel Kapoho Bay), and a micro aerial vehicle. The NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX communicates wirelessly with the x86 host computer. (C) Deployment and communication pipeline of the proposed system. Owing to the limited neuron models supported by Intel Kapoho Bay, the spiking perceptual representation module is deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, whereas the spiking navigation policy module is deployed on Intel Kapoho Bay. The Jetson Orin NX acquires the event stream and transmits control commands to the Pixhawk flight controller. The Jetson Orin NX and the x86 host computer exchange system information wirelessly. The x86 host computer exchanges spike trains with Intel Kapoho Bay through NxSDK.

Figure 3: Training pipeline of the proposed end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation method. Continuous grayscale image sequences are first transformed into asynchronous event streams using an event simulator. Depth estimation is then introduced as an auxiliary task to enable geometry-aware spiking features learning from event streams. The learned event features are fused with the MAV state and goal direction, and then encoded into spike trains via population coding. The resulting spikes are processed by the spiking navigation network and decoded to predict the action. Finally, collision loss, smoothness loss, and goal-reaching loss are defined based on the predicted action, providing physically meaningful supervision for end-to-end optimization of all network modules.

papers.abstract: Retrieval tasks are a form of search task where a robot must explore, find an object, and return with it as quickly as possible. Recent work in ergodic control has demonstrated time-optimal path planning for search tasks where visitation is proportionally matched, within some tolerance, to a given target distribution. However, these planners minimize the duration of a full deterministic search, while retrieval missions end their search at an unknown point in the trajectory and must return to a given base. In this work, we propose a new formulation of the time-optimal ergodic search problem that models detection as a Poisson process and minimizes total mission time by including the return phase in the objective. Experimental results show that time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER) achieves up to $19\%$ shorter mission durations relative to ergodic baselines and that this advantage grows as the return phase becomes more costly. Simulation and hardware implementations validate TOER's compatibility with environments of non-convex geometry as well as both 2D and 3D search domains.
authors: Christian Sulana, Christian Hughes, Ian Abraham
bullets: Addresses retrieval missions where detection occurs at an unknown point and the robot must return to a base.
Models object detection as a Poisson process and incorporates the return phase into the optimization objective.
Validated in simulation and hardware for non-convex environments and 2D and 3D search spaces.
Achieves up to 19% shorter mission durations than ergodic baselines, with larger benefits when returning is more costly.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Belief Fidelity Impact on Mission. Search in the room setting from Fig. 3 as the true target is displaced by δ from the given belief. (Left) InfoMax’s detection collapses once the belief is wrong (0.93 → 0.22) while the ergodic methods degrade slowly, since covering the belief’s support leaves detection mass where the target can still be found. (Right) TOER holds the lowest mission time until the target leaves the belief entirely, where its tradeoff between detection speed and terminal position is no longer beneficial.

Fig. 1. Time-Optimal Ergodic Retrieval. A Franka arm executes a full retrieval mission of a green block in an occluded 3D search domain. From its start pose (t0), the arm sweeps the bin along an ergodic trajectory (t1) until the overhead camera detects the target. Once detected, the arm abandons the remaining plan, grasps the object (t2) and delivers it to the base (t3). We propose time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER), which includes the expected return cost explicitly in the objective such that searches prioritize likely detection sites that are closer to the base.

Fig. 6. Computational Scaling of TOER. Log-log wall time for a single solve at fixed iterations (95% CI bands on each slope). TOER and TOES scale identically in trajectory knots N , while the Poisson detection term makes TOER grow linearly in domain samples M while TOES is sublinear.

Fig. 5. Return Bound and Detection Certificate. Validation of the return bound and detection certificate on the non-convex room grid from Fig. 3. (Left) The two return-cost estimates from one detection site. The obstacle-blind bound cuts through walls while the true geodesic routes around them. (Right, Top) Planning against the loose bound costs 0.1% of realized mission time relative to the geodesic bound. (Right, Bottom) With survival ≤ δ imposed, realized survival stays inside the certified region at every δ.

Fig. 2. Expected Mission Time Comparison. Single-target search in an open planar field as the sensor’s detection gain is swept at fixed κ = 6.6. When detection is unreliable, the target is usually not found, thus mission time is dominated by return, and TOES + Return suffers additional return cost at every unsuccessful episode. TOER holds a ≥ 12% advantage over TOES + Return throughout while matching TOES (End @ Base) without imposing a terminal constraint.

Fig. 3. Return Discrepancy Profile. Object search in a planar 12-room lattice. (Left) Search scene with uniform target draws and sensor footprint, occluded by walls. (Right) TOER’s paired mission-time advantage over each baseline vs. return discrepancy κ. Advantage grows logarithmically (R2 = 0.95) toward the ceiling from Prop. 2. The gap to TOER (search-only) isolates the return term, which is null at κ = 1 and 7.9% at κ = 10.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation is widely regarded as a more faithful way to assess end-to-end (E2E) driving models than open-loop evaluation, and Bench2Drive, built on the CARLA simulator, has become the dominant benchmark for it. We show that its evaluation protocol itself contains pitfalls that can misrepresent the models scored on it. Bench2Drive's comfort metric, adapted from nuPlan, has several implementation errors and a segmentation scheme that rewards standing still, so it mostly measures how long a vehicle stays stationary, correlating with stationary time at r = 0.97 across eight models. We propose a corrected, distance-based metric that cuts that correlation to r = 0.06. Under it, the strong driving-score/comfort tradeoff the original metric reports is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, which suggests that comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives. We also uncover two pitfalls in how the harness supplies navigation signals: the default controller can replace a model's own steering with an angle toward the route target point, and the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially from what a model saw in training. We demonstrate both on UniAD and VAD, where their effects differ sharply, and argue that future closed-loop evaluations should check for them. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from logged trajectories without re-running closed-loop simulation.
authors: Thomas Schwarzfischer, Emad Aghajanzadeh, Moritz Thoma, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
bullets: The original comfort metric contains implementation and segmentation flaws, with comfort strongly correlated with stationary time (r = 0.97 across eight models).
A corrected distance-based metric reduces this correlation to r = 0.06 and removes the apparent driving-score/comfort tradeoff when comparing models at matched speeds.
The reported tradeoff likely reflects driving speed rather than driving quality.
The evaluation harness may override a model’s steering with route-target guidance and provide target points that differ from training inputs.
The authors demonstrate differing effects on UniAD and VAD and release fixes that can recalculate comfort from logged trajectories.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Target-point distance supplied to UniAD in training and at evaluation time, on a logarithmic axis, with statistics (m) for both models below. The shaded band is the training p5 to p95 range, 4.06m to 6.60m, shared by both models. The original planner places UniAD’s target at a median of 64.6m, over an order of magnitude beyond the 4.94m training median, and behind the ego in 13.7% of frames. Ours restores the median for both models, to 6.28m and 6.09m. For UniAD it also removes the tail (p95 130.2m to 20.0m) and the behind-ego frames (13.7% to 0.9%); for VAD it does not, and we report that residual in section III-B.

Fig. 1. Illustration of two closed-loop evaluation pitfalls. In both panels blue marks the model’s own output: its predicted waypoints and the steering vector they imply. (a) Steering overruling: the red vector is the steering the controller substitutes, aimed at the navigation target point (red pin). This can mask a model’s failure to compensate its own steering error (left) and can override a maneuver around an obstacle (right). (b) Target-point mismatch: because the evaluation route planner samples the route differently than the planner that collected the training data, the navigation command switches at a different place along the route at test time (faded red pins) than during training (red pins). Here the ego receives turn right early and begins to rotate, then receives straight at the junction: the command calls for the straight continuation (purple) while its heading and the road geometry support completing the right turn (green), a command-context combination absent from training. Interpolating between the two can produce dangerous behavior. SO: steering overruling; TPM: target point mismatch.

Fig. 3. Sample route of SimLingo [3], showing driving speed over time together with the cumulative comfort scores of the different implementations. We re-project our distance-based implementation on the time axis. The traditional metric considers driving comfortable when and only when the ego vehicle is standing still, marked by the red shaded bands. Even the slight movement from seconds 35 to 38 is deemed uncomfortable. When we apply our fixes, the metric correctly scores segments when the vehicle is driving comfortably, but still incentivizes standing still. Further applying our distance-based segmentation fixes both problems, not changing the comfort score when the ego vehicle is stationary.

papers.abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.
authors: Jing Xia, Changyan Li, Yuduo Wang, Guiyin Tian, Bo Wang, Yifan Liao, Mingjun Li, Shiyan Hu

Combines human task constraints and environmental reports with robot-verified physical-state evidence.
Verified node arrivals support translational re-anchoring for visual depth point-goal navigation.
On a Unitree Go2, AVALON completed the reported mission in all 5 runs and avoided timeouts seen with policy-only X-NavDP.

papers.abstract: Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions. Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored. We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts. MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes. We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry. Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird's-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map. Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 2.60% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory. MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Hao Ju, Feng Yan, Zhihao Zhong, Heng Yang, Shaofei Huang, Zhedong Zheng

Augments navigation with pose-aligned depth memory projected into a Bird’s-Eye View occupancy map.

Reports a 2.60% success-rate improvement over existing methods; ablations support the value of spatial memory.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.
bullets: Represents collision risk using depth-normalized relative motion inferred from monocular optical flow.
Uses a Concurrent Learning observer to estimate normalized relative velocity and bound estimation error online.
Propagates uncertainty through angular inflation and a robot-footprint margin to construct a robust vision-based collision-cone control barrier function.
An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally adjusts nominal control to enforce safety.
In experiments, the error bound contained measured error in 98.3% of simulation samples, and TurtleBot3 completed 93/100 real-world trials without collisions.

An optimal-decay CBF-QP enforces the resulting safety constraint. papers.abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 {\mu}m. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 {\mu}m across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 {\mu}m spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.
authors: Kanhu Charan Andia, Harsh Prashant Katole, Parth Nitinkumar Bhosale, Hemant Kumar, Dhruv Pratap Singh
bullets: Real-time YOLOv11-based visual localization is combined with waypoint-based magnetic steering.

The microbots followed user-defined free-hand paths and navigated a physically confined maze.
A* planning enabled real-time replanning around multiple swimming micromotor obstacles.
The system supported selective cargo capture, transport, and delivery while avoiding dynamic obstacles.

papers.title: Vision-Guided Closed-Loop Autonomous Navigation of Light-Driven Janus Microbots
papers.tldr: A vision-guided, closed-loop system enables 3 μm light-driven Janus microbots to navigate complex and changing environments, avoid obstacles, and transport cargo autonomously.

papers.abstract: Geometric light detection and ranging (LiDAR)--inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) provides efficient state estimation but lacks the continuous map representation and global refinement capabilities of neural implicit SLAM, while neural implicit methods remain computationally expensive. We propose Lightweight LiDAR--Inertial Neural SLAM (LIN-SLAM), a hybrid method that couples high-rate geometric LiDAR--inertial estimation with neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement for accurate real-time onboard SLAM. Experiments on twelve representative sequences from three datasets spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) among the evaluated state-of-the-art geometric and neural implicit methods, while substantially reducing runtime compared with existing neural implicit SLAM methods. On a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a 16-channel LiDAR, LIN-SLAM sustains real-time localization and neural mapping over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory through challenging repetitive corridor environments, with an endpoint closure error of only 0.141~m. To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR--inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a mobile robotic platform while maintaining state-of-the-art localization accuracy. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Shiqi Che, Yijie Liu, Shuo Wang, Wenxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between efficient geometric SLAM and computationally costly neural implicit SLAM.
Uses high-rate geometric estimation alongside neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement.
Evaluated across twelve sequences from three datasets and multiple LiDAR configurations.
Reports the lowest overall mean ATE among evaluated geometric and neural implicit methods, with reduced runtime versus neural implicit baselines.
Runs online on a Unitree Go2 with a Jetson Orin NX over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory, achieving 0.141 m endpoint closure error.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the lightweight LIN-SLAM pipeline. A geometric generalized iterative closest point (GICP)–IESKF frontend processes LiDAR sub-sweeps and IMU measurements to provide local poses and motion-compensated scans. Full-sweep keyframe candidates associate geometry with source intervals, terminal poses, and covariances for asynchronous transfer. The neural implicit backend uses optimized C++/CUDA computation to reduce processing overhead, fixed-capacity replay storage and local neural windows to control stored data, and preallocated workspaces to reduce repeated allocation. Frontend relative motion initializes neural tracking; continual mapping and loop-based global optimization update the neural map. Backend corrections provide globally corrected poses at the frontend rate.

Fig. 2. Neural-SDF surface comparison on 64-channel Quad (top row) and 128-channel Math Institute (bottom row), using the same viewpoint within each scene. PIN-SLAM: (a), (d); CLID-SLAM: (b), (e); LIN-SLAM: (c), (f).
Fig. 4. Neural point maps produced during the onboard deployments: (a) Corridor and (b) Basement.
Fig. 3. Unitree Go2 platform used for the onboard experiment.

papers.abstract: Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap-7.github.io/MoCAP-page/.
authors: Yiyang Cai, Tatsuya Kamijo, Ninghao Lu, Zijin Hu, Sherry Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge from unstructured human videos to robots with different bodies and constraints.
Extracts spatial memory and human approach cues to guide object navigation and selection of manipulation-ready base poses.
Uses a closed-loop code-as-policy agent to coordinate planning and tool-use primitives under robot geometry and kinematic constraints.
On a real mobile manipulator, achieves 80% success on each of two indoor tasks where existing approaches fail.
Video-derived memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, while human approach priors improve reachable-base-pose discovery from 0% to 100% in an unfavorable start setting.

At task startup, an advisor VLM relates the spatial memory to the instruction and initial robot view. During execution, the system retrieves a recorded interaction with the target object and estimates where the person in the video stood relative to it from the frame preceding the reach. A closed-loop code policy coordinates navigation and manipulation through planning primitives that check actions against live geometry and robot constraints, revising execution from observations and feedback.
Fig. 4. Example executions of (a) grasping a cardboard box, (b) grasping a can, and (c) navigating to a blue trash bin. Keyframes in each row follow one continuous execution from left to right.

A coding agent uses them to find the target and reach a base pose with a feasible grasp. Grey dashed paths show execution without this prior.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots in warehouses and production facilities operate in precisely the environments that defeat point-feature visual odometry: featureless aisles, uniform walls, repetitive racking and specular floors. Such environments are, however, rich in straight-edge structure: rack uprights, door frames, wall junctions and cabinet outlines present high-contrast linear edges stable across wide viewpoint changes. A line-feature extension to cuVSLAM, a CUDA-accelerated visual-SLAM system, is presented that recovers this signal. Lines are parameterised as Pl\"ucker coordinates for geometric transport and as the minimal 4-DOF orthonormal representation of Bartoli and Sturm for optimisation; a Cauchy-robust point-to-line residual with analytic Jacobians is folded directly into cuVSLAM's per-frame Gauss-Newton pose solve, and the same line state is jointly refined in the Schur-complement sliding-window bundle adjustment. An adaptive information weight causes lines to assume more of the estimation burden exactly as point features become scarce, and the extension adds residual blocks to existing solvers rather than introducing a second estimator, reducing exactly to the unmodified point pipeline when disabled. Evaluated in RGB-D mode under SE(3) Umeyama alignment with no scale correction, line features reduce mean absolute trajectory error by 38.5% over the 22 sequences of the TUM RGB-D Freiburg3 collection and by 30.1% over the 8 Replica room and office sequences, where median translation error falls by 38.9% and median rotation error by 66.4%, with zero tracking failures in any configuration tested.
authors: Dara Molloy, Terry Wu, Wonju Lee, Abhilash Nand Kumar, David Adley, Conor Ferguson, Hesam Rabeti
bullets: Targets warehouse and production scenes where point features are sparse but straight structural edges remain reliable.
Represents and optimizes line features geometrically, integrating robust point-to-line residuals and analytic Jacobians into cuVSLAM’s pose solver and sliding-window bundle adjustment.
Adaptively increases line-feature influence as point features become scarce.
In RGB-D evaluations, reduced mean absolute trajectory error by 38.5% on TUM RGB-D Freiburg3 and 30.1% on Replica; no tracking failures occurred.
Scope: evaluated on 22 Freiburg3 and 8 Replica sequences under SE(3) alignment without scale correction.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Line-augmented cuVSLAM pipeline. The point path is unmodified; the line path runs in parallel and converges on the same Gauss–Newton pose solve, where λ(Np) of equation 9 shifts authority towards lines as point observations become scarce, and on the same bundle adjustment, where the minimal orthonormal parameterisation lets line landmarks marginalise by the same Schur complement already used for points.

Fig. 2. TUM RGB-D large cabinet validation: top-down trajectory (left) and APE translation over time (right). Points-only (red) accumulates drift to 0.18 m RMSE, while points+lines (blue) holds to 0.04 m by using cabinet edge lines as persistent drift anchors.

Fig. 3. LSD line detections (cyan) and point features (green) on TUM RGBD frames. Left, large cabinet validation: the flat, low-texture cabinet interior starves point detection while shelf and frame edges still yield long, welllocalised lines. Right, long office household: desk and monitor edges give clean lines alongside dense point coverage, the case where both modalities already agree.

Fig. 4. LSD line detections (cyan) and point features (green) on Replica frames. Left, room0: door and window-shelf frames and a wall-mounted grid provide stable line evidence over otherwise blank wall and floor. Right, office3: wall edges and furniture outlines anchor lateral drift where the wall carries almost no point texture.

papers.abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
authors: Wei-Jer Chang, Zhouchonghao Wu, Akshay Rangesh, Weixin Li, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses the need for realistic multi-agent traffic behavior without relying on human driving demonstrations or logged trajectories.
Jointly trains heterogeneous road users from random initialization using type-specific dynamics and objectives, procedural scenarios, and per-agent randomization.
Outperforms demonstration-free and prior demonstration-assisted self-play baselines on WOSAC while controlling all three road-user types.
Policies trained on nuPlan map geometry maintain comparable realism in zero-shot Waymo evaluation and outperform compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark.
Ablations show that heterogeneous self-play improves both realism and planning, especially in interaction-heavy scenarios.

The model consists of shared encoders followed by per-type LSTM cells, action heads, and value heads. Per-type rewards and value normalization accommodate distinct reward scales across road-user types. Each type uses its own dynamics model: jerk-integrated Ackermann dynamics for vehicles, unicycle dynamics for pedestrians, and kinematic bicycle dynamics for cyclists.

Unlike HR-PPO and SPACeR, which anchor self-play to demonstration-trained policies, SHRED uses no demonstrations, yet achieves the highest interactive score and higher realism than both, with greater rollout diversity. papers.title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
papers.tldr: SHRED learns realistic, interactive behavior for vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through heterogeneous self-play alone, without expert demonstrations.

papers.abstract: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
bullets: Closed-form bounds estimate arrival-point uncertainty, mesh coverage, packing limits, and the admissible repositioning commit window.
With non-overlapping agents, coverage is capped at 90.69% in 2D and 74.05% in 3D; overlap removes this separation-induced ceiling above a crossover of p=0.80.
Analytic placement reaches 85% of the applicable ceiling, whereas centralized PPO averages 15% across three training seeds.
Gaussian uncertainty is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but sensitive to bias: a one-standard-deviation aim-point offset reduces coverage by 14 percentage points.
The study validates its formulas by Monte Carlo and argues that feasibility ceilings should accompany learning results.

papers.abstract: Large datasets and high capacity models have accelerated progress in vision and language. This work introduces a platform aimed at bringing comparable gains to embodied learning, world models, and robotics. We present EnvDreamer, a framework that uses large language and vision language models to generate Unreal Engine 5 environments for embodied AI and robot training. EnvDreamer enables sampling of large, diverse, interactive, customizable, and validator passed virtual environments for training and evaluation across navigation, interaction, and manipulation. We illustrate the platform with a large set of generated scenes and simple baselines. Policies trained on EnvDreamer generated environments, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve competitive results on multiple embodied benchmarks spanning navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation. EnvDreamer also supports image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies. Finally, we release EnvDreamer-20k, a dataset of 20,000 validator passed environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata to support reproducible benchmarking.
bullets: Uses large language and vision-language models to create interactive, customizable, validator-passed virtual environments.
Supports embodied learning without explicit mapping or human task supervision, including navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation.
Policies trained in generated environments achieve competitive results across multiple embodied benchmarks.
Enables image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies.
Releases EnvDreamer-20k: 20,000 environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EnvDreamer system overview. The system builds environments from scratch using vision–language models (vLLMs) to plan and control Unreal Engine 5. User-provided text or image prompts along with system information such as Remote Control API commands and viewport screenshots (left) are passed to a vLLM-based Home Agent which decomposes the request into sub-tasks with Chain of ThoughtWei et al. [2022], generates a structured layout plan and task list in JSON, and compiles them into EnvDreamer API Python code for execution (middle). An Evaluator Agent then performs iterative task-completion checks on scene layout, furniture placement, and rationality, providing feedback until the environment passes validation (right). Finally, users can inspect the completeness of the environment by entering a play session in either an ego-centric or bird’s-eye view.

Figure 5: Task-conditioned dataset generation pipeline for EnvDreamer–20k. A user specifies a scenario by providing a prompt and a high-resolution viewport screenshot plus the current environment JSON description (left). A language model decomposes the request into a sequence of grounded sub-tasks such as “Walk to the kitchen” or “Put pizza on the plate” (middle). The system then checks which preconditions are satisfied by comparing object relations and automatically adding missing objects required to solve each task (e.g., placing a plate on the table). Finally, the validated environment details and the set of available tasks are exported as JSON and rendered through the EnvDreamer API to produce entries in the EnvDreamer–20k dataset (right).

Figure 7: High-level architecture of the EnvDreamer Remote Control API. Python clients issue JSON commands to AJsonSceneBuilder, which resolves assets, spawns actors, and returns structured responses.

Figure 2: Diverse and realistic floor plan generation with EnvDreamer. Unlike traditional procedural methods that rely on fixed generation pipelines with limited variation, EnvDreamer leverages language-driven synthesis to create diverse, realistic home layouts. Each layout shown was generated from natural language prompts (e.g., "Create a modern 2-bedroom apartment," "Design a spacious family home with open kitchen"), producing architectural arrangements that follows realworld constraints. The diversity spans from compact studios (left) to complex multi-room residences (right), with rooms color-coded by type: bedrooms (yellow), bathrooms (green), living areas (red), and other spaces. This prompt-based approach enables researchers to specify exact requirements for embodied AI and robotics experiments while maintaining architectural realism that fixed procedural pipelines struggle to achieve.

Figure 4: Interactive scene in EnvDreamer. Ego-centric view from the embodied agent with annotated object relations (on, under, between, near, inside) and a bird’s-eye view of the procedurally generated multi-room layout. The robot is rendered in-scene, and objects are spawned with realistic and diverse geometry, materials, and placements that afford navigation and manipulation.
Figure 8: Remote web session for EnvDreamer. The live UE5 viewport is streamed to the browser, while a simple builder UI issues layout updates through HTTP endpoints backed by the RC API.

Figure 3: Interactive prompt-driven environment editing with EnvDreamer. A GPT-5–based vLLM-based smart agent receives natural-language chat prompts from the user to constantly edit the environment, translates them into EnvDreamer API calls, and applies edits to a running UE5 scene over the web. Users can inspect the updated environment, accept or refine the changes, and leverage additional web-session tools such as restoring prior states, direct drag-and-drop editing, and image-instructed edits, while the system maintains a synchronized JSON representation of the scene.

EnvDreamer ships with a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arm for contact-rich manipulation tasks (left) and a Unitree Go1 quadruped for navigation and locomotion tasks (right). Both robots are spawned directly into procedurally generated EnvDreamer scenes and share a common sensor and action contract, making the dataset suitable for training general-purpose embodied policies.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital

A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.
Reaches 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one denoising step, near its ten-step score at 3.29× higher end-to-end speed; also reports 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 on navhard.

papers.abstract: We develop a self-supervised reinforcement learning algorithm that learns to build towers of up to eight cubes from scratch, without prior data, rewards, demonstrations, or pretrained models. Our method, Contrastive Planning via Spherical Linear Interpolation (C-Slerp), uses contrastive representations as reusable building blocks and repeatedly composes them to infer a sequence of intermediate waypoints. Under our hyperspherical parameterization, the learned representations allow intermediate waypoints to be inferred in closed form through spherical linear interpolation, without training a separate high-level policy or performing graph search. Importantly, the representation geometry also tells us how to adjust the number of waypoints based on the difficulty of each goal-reaching problem. Experiments show that our method succeeds on long-horizon navigation and robotic manipulation tasks, including settings where strong baselines fail to achieve a single success. Ablations further show that using a fixed number of waypoints substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of adapting the plan to task difficulty.

bullets: Learns from scratch in a self-supervised reinforcement learning setting, including tower-building tasks with up to eight cubes.

Adapts the number of waypoints to goal difficulty based on representation geometry.
Succeeds on challenging navigation and manipulation tasks where strong baselines may fail entirely; fixed waypoint counts perform substantially worse.

papers.abstract: Controlling an agent in an environment solely perceived through onboard vision is challenging: perception yields noisy, variable-length, and partially occluded context, while onboard compute is shared between perception and control, limiting the planning horizon executable in real time. We propose VIGOR-MPC, a modular student-teacher framework, agnostic to the perception pipeline, which addresses reference tracking across navigation tasks by distilling a privileged, field-of-view-aware long-horizon MPC into a computationally lightweight short-horizon MPC whose cost parameters are determined online from vision. The teacher operates in simulation with full state knowledge and a multi-trajectory formulation that guarantees the agent can stay within its field of view. The student observes only the noisy, occluded context produced by a perception module and learns, via a multi-level recurrent mapping, to infer cost parameters that aim to recover the teacher's behavior despite missing information. We evaluate VIGOR-MPC on vision-based autonomous racing in simulation and on hardware. Using only onboard perception of the track, VIGOR-MPC generalizes to tracks unseen during training and approaches the lap times of the privileged long-horizon teacher while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.
authors: Jelena Trisovic, Rahel Rickenbach, Marek Landert, Panagiotis Minos, Melanie N. Zeilinger
bullets: Addresses noisy, occluded, variable-length visual context and limited onboard compute in vision-based control.

Approaches the teacher’s lap times while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.
